NBA teams typically wait until the first-quarter mark of a new season to diagnose problems.

Who has that kind of time? Who needs that kind of time?

The 2026-27 campaign is barely two weeks old, and it's already possible to point toward a problem area for everyone. Granted, some of these might not be season-long issues, but plenty have the potential to become that if not properly addressed.

ATL | BKN | BOS | CHA | CHI | CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GSW | HOU | IND | LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN | NOP | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX | POR | SAC | SAS | TOR | UTA | WAS

With a slew of long-limbed stoppers and open-floor athletes, the Hawks can be all kinds of disruptive on defense and a terror in transition. But when they need someone to create something out of nothing against a set defense, the sledding can turn tough pretty quick.

Atlanta's half-court offense has managed just 0.91 points per play , per Cleaning the Glass. That's a bottom-third scoring rate across the Association (22nd).

Offensive creativity isn't exactly an on-paper strength for this roster, but the bigger issue so far might be a lack of spacing. Only two of the Hawks' five starters are clearing even 30 percent from three-point range.

When the Celtics swapped out Jaylen Brown for Paul George and draft picks this offseason, the prevailing thought was that this now clearly Jayson Tatum-led team had a chance to still be pretty good. Unspoken in that praise, of course, was that the expectation used to be greatness—not pretty goodness.

And if the Celtics are now just a single-star team, it's fair to wonder whether this group significantly lowered its ceiling over the summer.

Boston's 5-2 record and top-third net rating ( plus-6.7, ninth ) wouldn't show that, but the competition faced welcomes skepticism. So far, the Celtics have wins over the hungover Knicks, the struggling Magic and the lowly Nets and Bulls. Otherwise, they're 0-2 with a minus-24 scoring differential against the Pistons and Rockets.

The Nets have this season's youngest roster . They have seven different first-round picks from the past two drafts. This might be the youth-iest youth movement around.

Yet, their three minutes leaders are all in their age-27 seasons or older. Their offense runs first through 31-year-old Julius Randle and 28-year-old Michael Porter Jr.—two of the more logical trade candidates in the league. The developmental minutes and touches that could go to the young players are too often winding up with (arguably) veteran placeholders.

It might be one thing if this equated to a competitive formula for the club, but Brooklyn has one win in seven games and no discernible identity.

Ranking Every NBA Team's Top Trade Assets 💪

You know the basic premise of the sport? The whole put-the-ball-in-the-basket thing? Yeah, that's what the Hornets are having a tough time figuring out.

The Hornets rank dead-last in field-goal shooting (40.5 percent) and 29th in three-point percentage (29.6). While they're at least accurate from the free-throw line (81.5 percent, sixth), it's a wasted weapon, because they don't earn enough trips there to capitalize on it (30th in attempts).

The good news is things will get better with Coby White having just debuted and Kon Knueppel nearing the final stage of his hamstring strain recovery. The not-so-great news is that a lot of the bricklayers responsible for this clang-heavy start will remain big parts of the plan even when this group is full-strength.

Because the Bulls took such an agonizingly long time pulling the plug on their last (ostensibly competitive) core, they don't have nearly as many long-term resources in place as their fellow cellar-dwellers. Caleb Wilson already looks like a crown jewel, at least, and Matas Buzelis has his own hype train, but that might be it in terms of no-brainer building blocks.

So, while Chicago is taking all of the unavoidable lumps that come with an organizational reset, it lacks the abundance of hope sources a squad in this predicament would like to have. There is no obvious prize in front of the eyes, but there is the typical worry of what this level of losing can do to the psyche of a team.

The Bulls have tried to insulate their youth with some culture-setting veterans, but Norman Powell gets over his skis as a primary option, and Nic Claxton is stuck on the sidelines with a hamstring injury. Leonard Miller conquering consistency or Noa Essengue finding a niche would at least help build some long-term hope.

That's not a spelling error, folks. Rather, it's a creative-ish jab at the lack of offense—no "O"—from costly Cleveland newcomer Peyton Watson.

Remember, the Cavs sacrificed plenty to task the 24-year-old swingman with filling their hole at the small forward spot for good. Because he was a restricted free agent, they had to cough up Max Strus, a future first-round pick (unprotected) and a 2027 second-rounder for the right to give Watson a four-year, $88 million deal.

It's early, obviously, but Cleveland's return on investment has been nonexistent. Watson has unsightly shooting rates from the field (37.1 percent) and from three (16.7) and a ghastly net differential ( minus-25.7, seventh percentile , per Cleaning the Glass). Adding injury to insult, he also just missed a game with a hamstring issue—a worrying development given how much trouble his hamstring gave him last season.

Dallas Mavericks: The Disconnected Timeline

Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving have already produced some beautiful basketball in their short time together. It hasn't stopped speculation about an Irving trade, even as the Mavericks are telling teams "they don't even want to field your call," per NBA insider Marc Stein .

This is, by the sounds of it, all the result of outside noise. But outside noise still has a way of sneaking inside and uncomfortably lingering, especially when there's such an obvious reason for it to exist.

Flagg and Irving are a great basketball fit; they just happen to be an atrocious timeline fit. Flagg's 20th birthday will arrive only a few months before Irving's 35th. Maybe if the Mavs had everything they need to compete, they could justify trying to keep this duo intact, but they don't. This is mostly a young roster, as it should be given Flagg's long-term trajectory—which clearly doesn't align with Irving's.

The Nuggets are, almost by design, set up to struggle on the defensive end. They have more sieves than stoppers, which is why they haven't finished above the bottom-third in defensive efficiency since 2023-24.

And they're mostly OK with that. It's not ideal, obviously, but it's something they've been able to work around on the strength of their world-class offense.

But that's the issue: the offense isn't world-class right now. It's barely adequate, honestly, with Denver sitting a colossally disappointing 16th in offensive efficiency. A lot of factors play into that, including Nikola Jokić struggling with his range, and Cameron Johnson, Aaron Gordon and DeMar DeRozan all lacking their typical efficiency.

Stop me if you've heard this a time or 20, but Cade Cunningham could really use an offensive co-star. The Pistons don't even have an 18-point scorer alongside their MVP, and the only other player clearing 14 a night is shooting specialist Duncan Robinson.

Shout out to the pride of Williams College and all ( Go Ephs! ), but a contender counting on Robinson as the No. 2 option is not a contender that needs to be taken seriously.

This situation probably looks worse than it actually is—and it hasn't kept the club from racing out to a 6-1 start—since 2025-26 All-Star Jalen Duren has been sidelined by a hamstring strain. That said, concerns about scoring and creation help for Cunningham were raised even when Duren was making his All-Star ascension, so it might fall on the front office to find an external fix.

A five-game winning streak has quieted a lot of those doom-and-gloom tales of this team's demise spawned by its 0-3 start.

It has also showcased that this offense can be plenty potent with Stephen Curry doing Stephen Curry things, Yaxel Lendeborg casting an early ROY bid, Brandin Podziemski making shots and the bench getting buckets out of De'Anthony Melton, Brandon Williams and Georges Niang.

What this surge hasn't done, though, is solve some of the bigger questions about this defense. It lacks size on the interior and can run short of length and athleticism on the perimeter. Depending on the lineup configuration, it might be lacking in both at certain times.

If the offense isn't actually this good—it didn't crack 110 points in either of its first two contests—then the defense better not be this bad ( 22nd in efficiency , worst among teams with winning records).

Credit the Rockets for forcing me to get nitpicky here. Houston hasn't had the easiest schedule to start , but it definitely has made things appear that way. The Rockets have seven wins to show for eight trips to the hardwood, and they're sitting atop the entire league with a plus-12.8 net rating .

That makes problems hard to identify with this team, but it surely hoped for better shooting from guards Fred VanVleet and Reed Sheppard. Both are sitting below 39 percent from the field, and both are saddled with sub-32 three-point percentages.

They're still finding ways to impact winning, of course. The playmaking problems that plagued last season have all but evaporated, and the canyon these two have put between their averages in assists (10.8 combined) and turnovers (2.6) is a big reason why.

Indiana Pacers: Tyrese Haliburton's Hamstring

The Pacers had two big reasons to believe this season would be a lot more like their 2024-25 triumph (50 wins and an NBA Finals berth) than their 2025-26 misery (19 wins and brutal luck at the draft lottery). Well, it was really like two reasons rolled into one: the return of Tyrese Haliburton and his ability to weaponize new center Ivica Zubac.

Unfortunately, Haliburton's return from a torn Achilles lasted just four games before a strained hamstring got in the way. It's also, unfortunately, emblematic of the major injury issues Indiana has already encountered. On Monday, the Pacers became the first team since 1948 to use six or fewer players this early into a season.

They shouldn't be this banged-up again, but Haliburton's absence is the real worry. He gives this team an identity with his pace, penchant for passing and ability to come through in the clutch.

Since 2022-23, Haliburton's first full season in Indy, the Pacers have fared 4.2 points better per 100 possessions with him than without.

With Kawhi Leonard back north of the border, and Brandon Ingram yet to debut, the Clippers have zero margin for error on the offensive end. They are squeezed for scoring options with Darius Garland their lone player averaging 14-plus points.

So, they need to maximize the value of every possession. So far, they're doing the opposite. Only the shorthanded Hornets have a worse turnover percentage than the Clippers' 19.9 percent .

It's hard to blame Garland, when he's balancing primary scoring and table-setting duties, or Keaton Wagler, when he's a teenaged rookie, but they have been two of their worst offenders. Together, they're responsible for nearly eight giveaways a game.

The Lakers have built their offensive blueprint—if not their overall identity—around squeezing every ounce of production out of Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves.

And to an extent, the plan is working with Reaves posting personal bests in multiple categories, and Dončić averaging a wholly absurd 38.3 points.

"Obviously, he's one of the best scorers to play this game, if not the best," Giannis Antetokounmpo told reporters after being on the wrong end of Luka's latest 40-point outburst. "... Of all-time. I feel like some people are scared to say that, but he's got to be up there."

The worry, though, is what happens on nights when Dončić and Reaves don't have it rolling. The only other double-digit scorers are Walker Kessler (who gets spoonfed his scoring chances) and Ziaire Williams (who's shooting an unsustainable 47.6 percent from distance).

Quentin Grimes, Collin Sexton and Sandro Mamukelashvili need to be the scoring threats L.A. thought it was signing this summer.

It feels like a million and one unpredictable things have already happened this season. It also feels like Memphis' 6-0 start was the least predictable of the lot.

Even if you wondered whether this club could be feistier than expected, you didn't expect to see a juggernaut.

That's probably because, record aside, this really isn't a juggernaut. It could be a decent team, very possibly a play-in participant, but it's not this world-beater.

Rather, it's rolling due to some unsustainable shooting luck (42.2 percent from three compared to 31.2 by the opposition) and some monster outbursts from 29-year-old journeyman Ty Jerome (40-plus points in two games; 25 points on 27 shots in two others). Memphis will cool off at some point, and only then will folks see the real makeup of this team.

This should be Miami's best side. Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo comprise one of the most defensively versatile frontcourt combos ever created. Davion Mitchell is a dogged defender and a venomous head of the snake. Andrew Wiggins has been frustrating premier wing scorers for years.

This roster entered the season with significant questions about its ability to score and shoot from the perimeter. But so far, it's the defense holding back the offense. The Heat are sitting 27th in defensive efficiency , and the three teams behind them have three wins between them.

"We're not playing hard enough," Antetokounmpo told reporters after the Heat's 138-117 loss to the Lakers on Monday. "We've got to play hard, have some pride. Individual pride, first of all, and then we've got to keep one another accountable and trust one another defensively. Right now we don't trust one another. We're not giving that extra effort."

As painful as it was to trade away Giannis Antetokounmpo, the best player in franchise history, the Bucks have to be thrilled with what they've gotten back from the Heat so far.

Tyler Herro has near-star numbers, Jaime Jaquez Jr. looks efficient as ever, Kel'el Ware is almost averaging a double-double in under 20 minutes, and Kasparas Jakučionis is showing great feel on the ball.

Nearly all of Milwaukee's newcomers are finding a niche. The problem is the returning Bucks have mostly disappointed.

Kyle Kuzma has never been less accurate from three. Myles Turner isn't hitting shots from anywhere. Ryan Rollins looks like his 2025-26 breakout never happened. Ousmane Dieng hasn't forced his way into the regular rotation. Gary Trent Jr. isn't finding regular minutes, either.

Minnesota Timberwolves: Anthony Edwards' Knee

Over their first four games, the Timberwolves appeared well on their way to wearing the Best Show on Hardwood label.

They weren't just wildly entertaining with LaMelo Ball orchestrating the offense; they looked like legitimate contenders with the apparent impact this summer's changes had on Anthony Edwards.

And then, because the injury bug has serious main character syndrome this season, the run was over. For now, at least. Edwards had arthroscopic surgery on his right knee, and Minnesota hasn't been the same since.

The hope is the procedure happened early enough for Edwards to make it back in time to rediscover his form and help the Wolves howl come playoff time. The worry is they'll dig too big a hole without him, and he won't be the same after a lengthy layoff.

The Pelicans have lost four games this season. They had fourth-quarter leads in three of them and were down single-digits in the final four minutes of the other.

This team has enough talent to compete. It just may not have enough something—could be talent, could be direction, could be chemistry—to perform when it matters most.

New Orleans has so far made a mess out of late-game situations. This club is 1-3 in clutch games—five-point differential in the final five minutes—and holds a minus-16.8 net rating over 24 clutch minutes.

When the Knicks are at their best, they're a two-way force. Last season, while laying the groundwork for their drought-snapping championship run, they were one of four teams with top-seven efficiency ranks on offense and defense .

This season, they've got a decent defense ( 10th in efficiency ) and a pretty dismal offense ( 21st ). Uncharacteristic shooting woes feel like the primary culprit.

Jalen Brunson is shooting worse than 40 percent from the field. OG Anunoby is barely clearing 30 percent from deep. Mikal Bridges is barely involved in this attack (6.1 points per game) and looks awful when he is (30.8 percent shooting overall, 26.9 percent from three). The track records say they're due for a bounce-back, but this offense will continue to struggle until that happens.

What just happened to the Thunder feels too cruel to put into words. They were riding high as heavyweight title contenders, and then pow! : dislocated ankle and fractured fibula for Jalen Williams, torn labrum for Cason Wallace, patellar tendon tear for Chet Holmgren.

"This isn't a common situation, but it's our situation," team president Sam Presti put it .

Yet no roster, not even one as deep as this, can just next-man-up its way into replacements for an All-NBA swingman, an All-NBA 7-footer and an All-Defensive point-of-attack stopper. Holmgren should at least return around the new year, but the other two? Just hope for the best, I suppose.

Orlando has offensive issues. A lot of them. This isn't a good scoring or shooting team. Its stars have worrying redundancies in strengths and weaknesses. No one constantly wows as a creator or passer.

The challenge for the Magic, then, is to get as many bites at the apple as possible. But that might be where they're earning their worst marks. They aren't controlling the basketball ( 26th in turnover percentage ) or the glass ( 28th in rebounding percentage ).

So, they're left playing a math game the numbers say they can't win. They are averaging 105.4 combined field-goal and free-throw attempts; for their opponents, the average is 114.1. It might take best-in-the-business efficiency to overcome this gap, and Orlando is delivering nothing of the sort.

Philadelphia 76ers: Still Developing Chemistry

The 76ers are built to overwhelm opponents with star power and offensive eruptions. This NBA economic environment is designed to discourage superteams, yet Philly has fielded a starting five featuring two former MVPs and two All-NBA selections from last season.

Naturally, the Sixers are just steamrolling any and everyone in their path, right? Well, not exactly. In fact, they've been one of this season's worst first-quarter teams ( 26th in net rating ) and a pretty forgettable offensive team overall ( 19th in efficiency ).

The fact that this team still holds a 7-1 record (and a top-10 net rating ) speaks to what can happen when this kind of star power is assembled. Still, the Sixers are clearly finding their way with this new-look group. Them being this good while figuring things out on the fly highlights just how high their ceiling sits.

The Suns have dropped four of their first five games. They've also allowed at least 122 points in all but one. Even by modern NBA standards, that's a pretty obscene level of hemorrhaging points.

Now, there's surely some level of misfortune here. Phoenix's opponents are shooting 41.1 percent from three. That number almost assuredly won't hold.

But the Suns aren't helping themselves. They get sleepy off the ball. Their closeouts are too often late ( sixth-fewest shot contests ). Their ball pressure has been lax, too ( fifth-fewest deflections ). And they've been dreadful on the glass ( 30th in defensive rebounding percentage ). It's all bad.

Portland Trail Blazers: Atypical Shooting Woes

Complaints are hard to find—or even manufacture—for the Trail Blazers. Not even their most optimistic fans could've seen this coming: a 5-1 start with four road triumphs and a top-five net rating .

What might be most impressive, though, is that we aren't seeing the Blazers at their best.

Maybe they won't run an .833 winning percentage all season, but they also probably won't see Damian Lillard keep posting the worst field-goal percentage of his career, Deni Avdija keep shooting worse from the line than he has since his rookie year, or Scoot Henderson keep toting around a sub-35 field-goal percentage and sub-20 splash rate from three.

Sacramento Kings: Acuff's Neon-Green Light

The Kings are leaning into a youth movement that doesn't actually feature a ton of youth.

If they're losing faith in Nique Clifford (7.0 minutes a night), they might already be down to two keepers: Darius Acuff Jr. and Maxime Raynaud. And since the latter is sidelined by a knee injury, the former basically has free rein to run...well, everything.

Acuff is averaging 23.6 shots—as many as Luka Dončić and more than everyone not named Anthony Edwards. Acuff's 33.2 usage percentage is seventh-highest in the league. He is being utilized like a premier, heavy-volume producer.

He is not a premier, heavy-volume producer. Not as a 19-year-old rookie, at least. Acuff is shooting 40.6 percent from the field and 31.3 percent from deep. His assist-to-turnover ratio sits shy of the 2:1 mark you'd at least expect from such a high-mileage creator.

He is being given freedom to experiment with the full limits of his game, which could do wonders for his future, but might tank this offense in the present.

As soon as the Spurs committed to starting their three-guard lineup, concerns were raised about that trio's ability to maintain proper spacing. And those concerns have been validated—sort of.

San Antonio's starting five has been limited from long distance. That quintet has a collective 32.3 percent conversion rate, which ranks 20th among all starting groups. That's a tricky number to work around, even while this group has obvious perks for its playmaking, downhill finishing and chaos-creation on defense.

The surprising part of all this is that these struggles don't stem from the guards. In fact, De'Aaron Fox, Dylan Harper and Stephon Castle are all shooting better from three than they did last season. The problem is Victor Wembanyama (26.2 three-point percentage) and Devin Vassell (30) have seen the bottom drop out, and they were supposed to be the ones propping things up.

Much like his first trip north of the border, Kawhi Leonard's return to Toronto felt like the possible key to unlocking the team's championship potential. And given how much season remains, maybe it will wind up serving that exact purpose.

But after two uncharacteristically inefficient outings to start the season (39 points on 37 shots), he was forced off the floor by a familiar foe: inflammation and swelling in his knee. It's at least the left knee this time and not his historically problematic right one, but it's also the kind of injury that has an uncertain recovery time and always the chance for things to linger.

Toronto's contending hopes have been tied to Leonard's return as either a superstar himself or a rock-solid co-star for an ascending Scottie Barnes. If Leonard doesn't get right, this formula will never compute properly.

This was supposed to be the season when everything came together for the Jazz. They weren't chasing ping-pong balls anymore; they were seemingly ready to pair their up-and-comers with their already-establisheders and serve as, at least, a thorn in the sides of the NBA's elites.

Yet, nothing has gone according to plan—and you could argue that dates back to Walker Kessler's exit in restricted free agency. That left a void on the interior, and injuries have prevented Jusuf Nurkić from filling it. Jaren Jackson Jr.'s MCL tear further thinned the frontcourt, while the backcourt has hardly seemed ready to play winning basketball.

Utah is tied for the league's worst record and sits fourth from the bottom in net efficiency ( minus-11.7 ). In competitive terms, this club looks no different than the tankers of recent years, only this roster wasn't designed to chase draft lottery odds.

The Wizards knew life would be different this season, and a lot of the newness has been for the better.

Trae Young may not be worth what Washington is paying him, and Anthony Davis could wind up overpaid too, but you can understand why the front office brokered discounted trades for both. On the court, each is a clear need-filler.

These changes haven't been a true rising tide, though. Alex Sarr seems confused about how he's supposed to fit now. Tre Johnson is a shooting specialist who suddenly can't make shots. Will Riley, maybe the most interesting Wizard after the All-Star break last season, can't even find regular floor time.

Washington is searching for the right combinations, and this will take time given the huge organizational shift away from tanking and hopefully toward play-in competitiveness or better. Some of the youth might get lost in the shuffle, but the Wizards have a few too many young players still looking for answers.

articles.title: Ranking Every NBA Team's Top Trade Assets
articles.summary: It's way too early in the 2026-27 NBA season to be thinking about trades, but let's face it: You armchair GMs can't get enough of this stuff.
articles.body:
It's way too early in the 2026-27 NBA season to be thinking about trades, but let's face it: You armchair GMs can't get enough of this stuff.

Plus, to be fair, more than one squad is actually thinking transactionally. The Golden State Warriors need to figure out what to do with Kristaps Porzingis. Injuries leave the Oklahoma City Thunder with no choice but to search for outside help.

In that spirit, let's look at all 30 teams and determine their top three movable assets.

That'll require pretending the trade deadline is tomorrow and first asking whether a team wants to add a big-name talent or unload one for picks. That difference matters. Things will get very tricky when teams can go either way—something that'll come up often because, well, it's November .

Depending on the circumstances, a superstar player could be a trade chip or an untouchable centerpiece around which the team is trying to add supplemental talent.

From there, it's as simple as imagining what trade partners would be most likely to ask for in a deal.

No, it's not trade season at all. But let's pretend it is.

ATL | BKN | BOS | CHA | CHI | CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GSW | HOU | IND | LA Clippers | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN | NOP | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX | POR | SAC | SAS | TOR | UTA | WAS

2027 first-round pick (least favorable of MIL or NOP; protected 1-4)

Nickeil Alexander-Walker might be the most valuable contract in the league if you exclude max and rookie-scale deals. The Atlanta Hawks absolutely shouldn't trade a two-way starter who has developed into one of the best three-point shooters in the league, but that kind of talent on a $15 million-per-year salary could net a Mikal Bridges-like return.

If someone comes calling with three, four or five first-rounders on offer, Atlanta has to listen.

Jalen Johnson makes twice as much on an annual basis, but he's still underpaid for an All-NBA forward.

If the Hawks don't want to capitalize on those values by dealing their two best players for a superstar or draft haul, they'd better shop that 2027 first-rounder from either Milwaukee or New Orleans.

Most would agree the Celtics took a step back (at least from a "playoff ceiling" perspective) by dealing Jaylen Brown over the offseason, but they still seem more likely to profile as buyers than sellers.

That puts the 2031 first-rounder they got from the Sixers for Brown in play alongside their own 2031 first-rounder.

Payton Pritchard's recent extension means he can't be traded for six months. Another team might have viewed him as a piece worth pursuing at an average annual value of $15 million per year through 2029-30, but buyers might instead have to aim for Derrick White, who has three years and $98 million left on his current contract.

There's a ton to like here, as the Brooklyn Nets will benefit from the eventual demise of the New York Knicks and the Denver Nuggets. Though that Nuggets pick is a long way off, Brooklyn is poised to capitalize if the Knicks fall apart at any point during the next half-decade.

In addition to the 2029 and 2031 picks, the Nets also have New York's 2027 first-rounder—not to mention a top-eight protected 2028 first from the Sixers.

The smart move would be to keep most of those and rebuild through the draft, which would put the likes of Michael Porter Jr. and Julius Randle into the trade mix ahead of those selections. If anyone's calling Sean Marks, they'll ask about those picks first.

Naz Reid isn't here because he failed to meet head coach Charles Lee's organizational standards. He's here because he's a plus starter and will make less than 15.0 percent of the cap through 2029-30. A player who can spread the floor and attack off the dribble from a frontcourt spot is always in demand.

The Hornets would obviously shop him long before considering Kon Knueppel or Brandon Miller.

If the Hornets go the other way and want to ship out future assets for immediate help, those 2033 firsts from Minnesota and (especially) Phoenix are true golden tickets. Maybe the Wolves will still be respectable seven years from now, but nothing about the Suns suggests we can count on competency.

The current regime didn't choose Matas Buzelis, which puts him in more trade jeopardy than you'd expect for a young, talented forward on a rookie-scale deal. He'd net bigger potential returns than Powell or Jones, both productive players with the added bonus of no guaranteed money beyond this season.

Powell, in fact, seems to have been signed as a trade chip. He's earning $21.5 million this season and has a team option for next year. Any team that needs shooting (and doesn't care about defense) could target him and revel in the flexibility of that team option.

Jones is more of a fringe starter, but he's in his prime at 27 and has a team option for $8 million next year.

Something significant will have gone wrong with the current core if Mobley's name winds up in trade talks, but he'd clearly be the Cavs' most in-demand commodity in that hypothetical.

Given the length of Donovan Mitchell's new extension, the likely lack of interest in James Harden and Jarrett Allen's "meh" standing among starting centers, Mobley is the one piece that could replenish the war chest in the event of disaster.

More realistically, the Cavs would shop their 2033 first-rounder, which is the only one they're allowed to trade. Peyton Watson could be a "last in, first out" option if the Cavs decide they need to split his deal into a couple of smaller ones for depth.

The incoming 2029 first-round pick from the Clippers would lead most packages in a hypothetical win-now Mavericks trade, a scenario that seems more likely than many expected. Cooper Flagg, already playing at All-NBA levels in his second season, might be good enough to coax some shorter-term thinking out of the new front office.

A more measured path involves dealing Irving, who has one more year at $42 million (player option) on his current deal but doesn't fit with the Mavs' Flagg-based timeline.

Lively may have no market whatsoever until he proves he can stay healthy. Still out while recovering from foot surgery, the No. 12 pick in 2023 would be an intriguing target for a team interested in making him a "second draft" rehab project. His health makes him a very high-upside long shot.

Any discussion of the Nuggets' trade assets is obliged to include Zeke Nnaji, who still somehow has another year and $7.5 million (player option) on his contract. But just because he's been expendable from the moment he signed that extension doesn't mean other teams are actually interested.

If they did, Nnaji, out of the rotation for years, would have been gone a long time ago.

Denver got Cleveland's 2031 first-rounder in exchange for Peyton Watson and could use it to add to the current team—if it had any substantial matching salary it could afford to lose. As it is, the Nuggets really can't improve (even if attaching that future first) without sacrificing vital pieces of the core in the form of Aaron Gordon or Jamal Murray.

Desperation hasn't reached those levels yet, so Johnson and his expiring $23 million make the list instead.

It's pretty simple for the Detroit Pistons, who won 60 games a year ago and intend to do something similar (hopefully with more playoff success) this time around. Led by Cade Cunningham and newly paid supporting pieces Jalen Duren and Ausar Thompson, Detroit is trying to win a championship.

Remarkably, for a team with that goal, the Pistons are still in control of all their own future first-round picks. If they trade one, an acquiring team would probably prefer it as far out as possible because Detroit's young core suggests plenty of success over the next handful of years. By 2033, maybe a 31-year-old Cunningham will have started to slow down.

Robinson and Collins both have non-guaranteed money on the books after this season, making them ideal salary matches. Attaching both to a future first would let Detroit bring back a player making nearly $40 million.

The Warriors have all their own future first-rounders, except for a top-20 protected 2030 selection that they have a good chance of keeping anyway. Trade partners face a tough choice if given their pick of future first-round assets.

Golden State is going to be in big trouble whenever Stephen Curry is gone, but the team isn't exactly blowing the doors off right now either. It wouldn't be the worst gamble to aim for the Dubs' 2027 first. If Curry gets hurt this season, the Warriors would immediately rank among the five worst teams in the league. Target a selection in the 2030s, believing the organization will have already rebuilt by then.

Porzingis' deal is only guaranteed for $3 million next season, while Butler's massive $57 million salary is expiring. It's possible neither plays this year due to illness and injury recovery, respectively. That's a mountain of matching salary to pair with picks if Golden State seeks a big name on a long-term deal.

For a team that looks capable of finishing first in the West, the Houston Rockets sure have a lot of high-value flippable assets. If they eventually decide a core of Amen Thompson and Alperen Sengun can't hack it in the playoffs, they have the tools to change their makeup.

That starts with a trio of incoming future firsts from teams that figure to finish with two or three ping-pong balls in the new lottery system. Brooklyn and Phoenix are well on their way to finishing as bottom-five teams this season, which means Houston's only real concern is that one or both are so bad they land in the relegation zone.

Those picks are hugely valuable either way, as is the swap coming from Dallas or Phoenix in 2029. Houston can attach salary to any of those selections and immediately attract a trade partner that wants in on a ton of potential draft upside.

Like the Warriors, the Indiana Pacers control all of their own future first-rounders. If there was a silver lining in their 2026 selection (which became Keaton Wagler) conveyed to the LA Clippers, it's that it eliminated the possibility of the Pacers owing their 2031 pick. That would have made it a bit more complicated to send out multiple future firsts due to the Stepien rule.

As it is, Indy can send out any first between 2027 and 2033. The tricky part is finding a non-essential salary to attach.

Walker hasn't popped since the Pacers grabbed him at No. 8 in 2023, but his youth and the control his restricted free agency brings this summer could have some appeal. Nesmith fits anywhere, though an acquiring team might not love that his $11 million salary this season jumps to $19 million in 2027-28.

Derrick Jones Jr. leads a handful of mid-priced vets the rebuilding Clippers should strongly consider shopping. His expiring $10.5 million salary is a bargain, as he's provided two-way value for playoff teams in the past.

Though perhaps not worth a first-rounder in a trade on his own, Jones could be paired with any of Max Strus ($16.7 million), Brook Lopez ($9.2 million and Kris Dunn ($5.6 million) to send out a ton of expiring money.

LA shouldn't have any interest in giving up the first-rounders it got from Toronto for Kawhi Leonard...unless there's a superstar who wants to make his home in Southern California. In that unlikely event, LA could attach those to Brandon Ingram or Darius Garland in a blockbuster move.

The Lakers put everything that wasn't nailed down into the package for Walker Kessler, so their only movable first-round asset is a distant 2032 swap. At this point, with so much draft equity out the door, it might actually make some sense to just fire off the rest of it. A team this committed to the current core might as well just go all the way in.

Of course, that strategy only makes sense if the right player becomes available. Even then, the Lakers are woefully short on non-essential players to send out in a trade. Hardy and Vanderbilt come closest, though the latter might not be a positive-value asset on his own.

Los Angeles made its move in the offseason. With so little to offer, this team is going to sink or swim with what it has.

It might seem like a fireable offense to trade Ty Jerome, who's spent a good chunk of the early season playing like an All-NBA guard. Then again, his inability to stay healthy over the years might make this the right time to strike. Even Jerome's staunchest proponents have to admit he's well outside the Grizzlies' timeline at age 29.

Given the Grizzlies' strong start, though, it wouldn't be ridiculous for them to be careful buyers. If that's how things go, they can put incoming firsts from Phoenix and Orlando on the table, perhaps packaged with Grant's $34 million salary.

Wait, didn't the Heat just acquire Giannis Antetokounmpo?

Look, we're just dealing with reality on its own terms here. If things continue to go as poorly as they have so far for Miami, the only real way out of this is flipping Giannis again.

That's obviously a disaster scenario, but it's hard to imagine the Heat ever trading Bam Adebayo and harder still to concoct a deal for an upgrade using the meager assets on hand. The Heat aren't going to blow things up by trading Giannis, but they genuinely don't have a way to add more talent after giving up so much to get him in the first place.

The Bucks aren't likely to trade picks of any kind, but that 2031 pick coming from Miami has too much upside to ignore. If Milwaukee wants to get anyone's attention, it could attach that choice future first to Herro's expiring $33 million and watch the offers roll in.

Odds are the Bucks will instead take back bad money with picks attached if they move Herro, but getting off Turner's deal (three more years and $83 million) might change the dynamics. If he doesn't start to show some of his Indiana form, Turner could become a truly negative asset that requires draft compensation to move.

Kyle Kuzma ($20.5 million) and Caris LeVert ($14.8 million) are both expiring and could provide salary relief to capped-out trade partners. They're far more likely to move than any of the younger, rookie-scale pieces from the Giannis deal.

The Wolves don't have many draft assets left after using most of what they had to acquire LaMelo Ball. What few remain, led by a 2032 first-round swap, may need to be on the table.

That's the cost of thinning out the roster and then losing Anthony Edwards to knee surgery. Depth was already an issue. Now, it's a critical one.

DiVincenzo (expiring $12.5 million) might appeal to someone who wants his Bird rights. The sweet-shooting guard tore his Achilles last spring and may not contribute this year, but he might be a free-agent retention priority for an acquiring team.

Shannon is even more valuable now than he was before Edwards' injury, as he's one of the few Minnesota players who can cave in a defense off the dribble. His youth, upside and motor also appeal to the rest of the league.

2027 first-round pick (most favorable of NOP and MIL; protected 1-4)

The New Orleans Pelicans probably should have already traded Murphy. Their refusal to use/showcase Herb Jones until injuries required them to do so remains confounding. In the event the Pels figure out they need a fresh start around Jeremiah Fears (and maybe Derik Queen), those two will have robust markets.

That 2027 first-rounder probably shouldn't be on the table, but we know the Pelicans will fire their future picks into the sun if there's a player Joe Dumars and/or Troy Weavers like. That strategy didn't burn them on draft night in 2025, but it was still bad process.

Pels fans should be concerned that the front office is emboldened by how that deal with the Hawks turned out. If we could assume Dumars and Co. won't act irrationally again, we'd slot Dejounte Murray into the place held by that 2027 selection.

You're not exactly supposed to be asset-rich after you win the title, so it's no surprise the New York Knicks are short on picks to send out for near-term help. That said, they can still shop their last outright tradable first in 2033, along with a pair of swaps. Not bad!

Karl-Anthony Towns is the answer to "which one of these doesn't belong" on New York's asset list, but the lack of a preseason extension and the sheer size of his contract make him a worthwhile inclusion. The Wolves dealt him to New York for two smaller contracts to increase flexibility and avoid paying him; maybe the Knicks will eventually choose to do the same.

Perhaps it seems like nobody would want KAT and the looming specter of his $61 million player option for 2027-28, but if New York offered Towns to the Warriors for Jimmy Butler and a pick, the Dubs would very likely pull the trigger.

2027 first-round swap (LAC; protected 1-5)

2029 first-round swap (DEN; protected 1-5*)

There are drastic scenarios in which the injury-riddled Oklahoma City Thunder retrench and further cut costs by sending out a piece of their core. Those are unlikely, so we're not getting into hypotheticals about Chet Holmgren, Ajay Mitchell, Alex Caruso or anyone else.

OKC is far more likely to address the depth issues created by injuries to Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace by tapping into its considerable draft resources. The Thunder's own picks, which they control, won't be that valuable. The swap rights they have on firsts in the next three drafts could be, though.

If Sam Presti does anything consequential, potential incoming firsts from the Clippers, Mavs and Nuggets will be involved.

*If DEN conveys its 2027 first-round pick

The Orlando Magic are wildly expensive and may reach a point where they must choose between Suggs and Black. The former is more established and earns an average of $29 million through 2029-30, but comes with injury concerns. The latter is set to hit restricted free agency after earning $10 million this year.

The takeaway: Orlando probably can't afford to keep both.

After that, the Magic's own 2032 selection would command some interest as a sweetener.

If there's a larger shakeup on the horizon, Wagner is much more likely to head out than Paolo Banchero. Much like Suggs and Black, those two max-salary forwards might be approaching a "this town ain't big enough for the both of us" crossroads.

2029 first-round swap (LAC; protected 1-3)

The Clippers are almost certainly going to struggle for the next two seasons, adding real upside to that 2028 first-rounder. If the Sixers want to make another addition to their starry core, that asset will almost certainly be in play.

Given the short-term shelf life of a roster that includes Joel Embiid and LeBron James, the wiser move would be to hold onto that pick and the 2029 swap coming in from LA. But Philly is chasing a ring and might be persuaded to double down.

Edgecombe is a potential star on a rookie-scale deal. He's also a key piece of the team right now. That said, he'd draw major interest from the rest of the league and is far more likely to be moved than any of Tyrese Maxey, Jaylen Brown, James, or Embiid.

Nobody's in worse shape, asset-wise, than the Phoenix Suns, a team that recently saw fit to send out its unprotected 2033 first-rounder for Miles Bridges. That was one of the worst deals any team made this past offseason. It's indicative of this organization's total disregard for long-term thinking.

So while it seems ridiculous to consider putting that 2032 swap on the table, and while no right-thinking team would entertain the idea of shipping out its best young prospect (Maluach) and valuable shooter (Gillespie), you can't rule anything out with the Suns.

The Portland Trail Blazers' acquisition of Ja Morant was opportunistic and achieved at a low cost, but it was also a suggestion that short-term success is the objective.

That makes Holiday's inclusion seem strange, but he has universal two-way appeal to contenders and is only under contract for one more year (at $37.2 million, which stings) after this one. It might seem more sensible to choose Scoot Henderson, but he's shown nothing this season to suggest he's a future star.

The swap from Milwaukee and the unprotected first from Orlando are the real gems here. Attach those to Holiday's salary, and something good's coming back the other way.

Technically, the Sacramento Kings' own first-rounders are their top assets. We'd normally lead the list with those because the Kings have never been shy about mortgaging their future for short-term gains.

Because Sacramento seems to understand it's going nowhere, we're assuming it won't put any of its own valuable picks on the table and will instead look to move its best incoming selection. That'd be the Wolves' unprotected 2031 first-rounder.

After that, it gets bleak. Murray has gotten worse every year since he was a rookie. Hunter is only valuable because his $24.9 million salary comes off the books after this season.

Domantas Sabonis and Zach LaVine are much more likely to be bought out than traded.

The San Antonio Spurs aren't going to deal any of their top young talent, which means Victor Wembanyama, Dylan Harper and Stephon Castle are all staying put. The success that trio is likely to produce devalues the Spurs' own picks. That incoming 2031 swap from the Kings is the team's juiciest draft chip.

De'Aaron Fox isn't an optimal fit, but he's grossly overpaid and probably not movable for positive value.

Of the other assets teams might covet, the Spurs could put Atlanta's unprotected 2027 first on the table, attached to Johnson's expiring $18 million salary. That should be enough for the kind of win-now upgrade we'd expect San Antonio to seek.

Barrett's expiring $29.6 million salary is basically the backbone of any potential Raptors move. We should assume that, based on the summer acquisition of Kawhi Leonard, the goal would be short-term gains.

To accomplish that, Toronto may need to attach its only tradable first-rounder in 2029. Leonard, Scottie Barnes, Collin Murray-Boyles and Allen Graves are off limits.

Walter is just here because he's on the rise. His rookie-scale deal would give an acquiring team significant control over his future. Toronto shouldn't have any interest in moving him, but he has real value and could combine that 2029 pick to significantly sweeten a deal.

Utah has plenty of young talent in Ace Bailey, Darryn Peterson and Keyonte George. The first two are part of the core. The third just inked a $150 million extension over the summer. None of them are on the table.

While the Jazz could consider shopping Jaren Jackson Jr. or Lauri Markkanen in bigger shakeups, the far more likely course involves dangling the Lakers picks that came over for Walker Kessler. The further out you go, the more likely Luka Dončić is gone or in decline.

That makes the unprotected pick in 2033 the crown jewel of Utah's considerable trove of assets.

The Wizards never gave Davis an extension, which means they're not fully committed to making him part of their core. That's the right call. It would have been wise to treat Trae Young the same way, but you can't win them all.

A healthy Davis is probably worth a first-rounder at the deadline, even heading into his $63 million player option for 2027-28. George is maximally scalable and would have real appeal to any team willing to send back a win-now piece.

Lastly, every future Suns asset is worth its weight in gold.

Stats courtesy of NBA.com , Basketball Reference and Cleaning the Glass . Salary info via Spotrac .

Grant Hughes covers the NBA for Bleacher Report. Follow him on Bluesky and subscribe to the Hardwood Knocks podcast, where he appears with Bleacher Report's Dan Favale .

articles.title: La NBA vuelve a plantearse reducir los partidos a 40 minutos para prevenir las lesiones
articles.standfirst: El frenético ritmo de juego y calendario provocan numerosas bajas y el comisionado Adam Silver está estudiando implementar en el futuro una idea que hace años que se escucha
articles.summary: El frenético ritmo de juego y calendario provocan numerosas bajas y el comisionado Adam Silver está estudiando implementar en el futuro una idea que hace años que se escucha
articles.body: En la noche del pasado 28 de octubre, hubo 80 jugadores de la NBA en la lista de bajas de sus respectivos equipos. Eso supone un 15% del total. Y eso, en la segunda semana de competición. Ante la sucesión de lesiones que viven los jugadores, la Liga está analizando distintas opciones para reducir la carga física de los jugadores y proteger su salud mientras los partidos tienen un ritmo endiablado que obliga a los protagonistas a enormes esfuerzos. La solución que parecería más lógica, reducir el calendario de 82 encuentros de temporada regular, es inviable, pues supondría un recorte en los ingresos de las franquicias por derechos de televisión y entradas. Además, eso afectaría también a los salarios de los jugadores y a nadie le agrada que le toquen el bolsillo. Así que ha vuelto a cobrar fuerza una idea que se escucha desde hace años: la posibilidad de reducir la duración de los partidos a 40 minutos, como en el baloncesto FIBA, en lugar de mantener los 48 actuales. Según algunos medios estadounidenses, el comisionado Adam Silver estaría estudiando esa opción. Como en el caso anterior, también tendría sus inconvenientes. Por ejemplo, a menos minutos, los propietarios de la franquicias podrían exigir recortes en los salarios de los jugadores. Además, el tiempo para espacios publicitarios, otra fuente de ingresos, sería igualmente menor. Hay quien cree que, además, esa medida no reduciría demasiado los minutos de las estrellas, sino que afectaría sobre todo a los jugadores de rotación. Los titulares seguirían jugando por encima de la media de hora mientras que el resto sí que sufriría un tijeretazo a su tiempo en pista debido a que se jugarían ocho minutos menos y no habría para todos. Eso podría hacer que las plantillas acabaran acortándose al no necesitar tantos efectivos. Y otro aspecto muy importante sería el de las estadísticas y los récords. La NBA es una competición que da gran peso a los números y es evidente que no se pueden alcanzar los mismos en partidos a 40 minutos que en 48. Si se implanta esa medida, todas las cifras desde entonces deberían llevar un asterisco en los libros de historia. Mientras la NBA busca una solución para un problema tan grave, los aficionados ven cómo esta temporada ya han caído Anthony Edwards, Ja Morant, Kawhi Leonard, Jalen Williams, Tyrese Haliburton... Un alarmante goteo de ausencias de estrellas que perjudica al espectáculo y a la competición.

articles.title: 7'5 5-Star Center Cherif Millogo Makes Commitment Decision Between Kentucky, UNC, Texas, More
articles.summary: Class of 2027 star center Cherif Millogo will be taking his talents down South to start his college career.
articles.body:
Class of 2027 star center Cherif Millogo will be taking his talents down South to start his college career.

On Wednesday, Millogo announced that he is committing to Kentucky over offers from UNC, Texas and others. The 7'5" big man, who is rated as a 5-star prospect and the No. 6 center in 247Sports' composite , is head coach Mark Pope's highest-ranked recruit with the Wildcats.

In his evaluation of Millogo, Jack Pilgrim of On3.com described him as "the most physically imposing big man in the country, agile for his size and capable of knocking down jump shots, but also an impossible load to handle in the frontcourt. Boasting a 7-foot-9 wingspan, Millogo is a vicious rim protector with tremendous upside as he improves his strength and conditioning and continues stacking game reps."

Millogo is now one of the headliners of a 2027 Kentucky recruiting class that also includes small forward Ryan Hampton, who is rated as a 5-star prospect and the No. 7 player at his position in 247Sports' composite . The young duo should fuel optimism for a bright future under Pope, who has led the Wildcats to back-to-back NCAA Tournament appearances in his first two years at the helm.

Landing Millogo continues the good vibes in Kentucky after the team opened the 2026-27 season with an 85-57 win over Manhattan on Tuesday night. Senior forward Milan Momcilovic dropped 24 points to lead the Wildcats, who are starting the year ranked No. 23 in the AP Top 25.

Kentucky will be back in action on Friday in another home matchup against James Madison.

articles.title: Nikola Jokic's Trade Status Discussed by NBA Exec Amid Nuggets' Struggles to Start 2026 Season
articles.summary: Amid a 3-3 start to the season for the Denver Nuggets after an offseason that was roundly criticized for not trying to maximize the talent around their superstar center, Nikola Jokić's status is being closely monitored around the NBA.
articles.body:
Amid a 3-3 start to the season for the Denver Nuggets after an offseason that was roundly criticized for not trying to maximize the talent around their superstar center, Nikola Jokić's status is being closely monitored around the NBA.

As one NBA executive told The Ringer's Howard Beck , the 29 teams outside of Denver are "not doing their job" correctly if they aren't at least thinking of ways to get Jokić.

"Twenty-nine executives are not doing their job if they're not constantly thinking about how to get Jokić on their team," the exec said.

Ranking Every NBA Team's Top Trade Assets 💪

Jokić, who is in the final season of his current contract, said in September he plans to sign a new deal with the Nuggets next summer.

There is financial incentive for Jokić to wait because he can sign for up to five years and $359.5 million. If he extends off his current deal, he would be limited to a four-year contract worth up to $278 million.

However, waiting does also raise the question of how appealing the Nuggets will look to Jokić by the time they get to the offseason.

Coming off a first-round playoff loss last season, the Nuggets' summer included losing Peyton Watson in a sign-and-trade with the Cleveland Cavaliers, losing Tim Hardaway Jr. in free agency and using the waive-and-stretch provision to move on from Jonas Valančiūnas.

The primary additions in Denver were DeMar DeRozan and Marvin Bagley III.

B/R's Grant Hughes graded the offseason moves for all 30 teams prior to the start of the regular season. Denver's grade of D-minus was tied with the Washington Wizards for second-worst, ahead of only the Los Angeles Clippers with an F.

Watson is off to a slow start in Cleveland so that move may not look as egregious in hindsight, but the lack of any significant addition to support a strong trio of Jokić, Jamal Murray and Aaron Gordon has the Nuggets looking rather sluggish right now.

"They've obviously struggled to build around him since the championship because of the financial constraints," an executive told Beck. "Do they finally just say: All right, he's 31 now; do we just pull the trigger because he's got a huge extension coming up this summer, and then it's going to be even harder to build around the guy?"

The Nuggets are 3-3 through their first six games, but they rank 16th in offensive rating and 23rd in defensive rating. They are the only team at .500 or better with a negative net rating (minus-2.9).

Denver hasn't finished a season outside of the top 10 in offensive rating since Jokić's rookie year in 2015-16.

There has been no indication from Jokić's side he is looking to leave the Nuggets, so perhaps any potential trade or free-agent speculation will end up meaning nothing.

But the way this season has started isn't easing any of the concerns about how Denver's roster looked after a disappointing summer for the franchise.

articles.title: Warriors Reportedly 'Not Delivering Payments' to Kristaps Porzingis as Star Contemplates NBA Future
articles.summary: As veteran center Kristaps Porzingis continues to contemplate his future in the NBA, the Golden State Warriors reportedly haven't sent him a paycheck this season.
articles.body:
As veteran center Kristaps Porzingis continues to contemplate his future in the NBA, the Golden State Warriors reportedly haven't sent him a paycheck this season.

According to ESPN's Shams Charania and Anthony Slater, the Warriors are "not delivering payments" to Porzingis on his $20 million salary for this year, ruling that he is not rendering services. The team reportedly "will continue exhausting trade avenues as the 31-year-old leans toward ending his NBA career."

Ranking Every NBA Team's Top Trade Assets 💪

ESPN's Bobby Marks noted that Porzingis is losing $218,341 per game due to his failure to render services, and his salary still counts against the cap and tax apron.

Slater reported that league sources said Porzingis is "not actively disputing the lack of payments." Team sources added that the Warriors "have no current plans on voiding Porzingis' contract... maintaining trade flexibility up until the Feb. 11 deadline."

Porzingis has been away from the Warriors for this entire season while dealing with what is described as a personal medical issue. The 31-year-old re-signed with Golden State on a two-year, $40 million contract this past offseason. However, only $3 million of his salary for the 2027-28 season is guaranteed, making it easier to trade him. Charania noted that "absorbing Porzingis' near-expiring deal would allow a rival team to move a salary out and save money and clear a roster spot via a buyout," which would give the big man the chance to recoup some of his lost wages.

However, NBA insider Jake Fischer reported that Golden State "knows that trade interest is unlikely to materialize immediately." The Warriors faced a similar situation two seasons ago when guard De'Anthony Melton tore his ACL early in the 2024-25 campaign, which led them to trade him for veteran guard Dennis Schroder, who was then flipped two months later to acquire star wing Jimmy Butler III.

Sources told Fischer that Golden State "hopes to do something similar with Porzingis to try to add a serviceable frontcourt player on an expiring contract. Ideally such a deal is consummated by Dec. 16 so the incoming player, like Schröder before him, can be re-aggregated with other contracts in a subsequent trade before the Feb. 11 trade deadline."

It sounds like there won't be a resolution anytime soon, but Porzingis' time with the Warriors will likely come to an end at some point.

articles.title: Giannis-Bam Pairing Ripped by NBA Exec amid Heat's Early-Season Struggles
articles.summary: Back-to-back wins apparently haven't been enough to assuage doubts about Giannis Antetokounmpo's fit alongside Bam Adebayo with the Miami Heat.
articles.body:
Back-to-back wins apparently haven't been enough to assuage doubts about Giannis Antetokounmpo's fit alongside Bam Adebayo with the Miami Heat.

The Ringer's Howard Beck reported "league insiders remain highly skeptical of the Adebayo-Antetokounmpo pairing" after the Heat's 2-5 start to the 2026-27 season.

One NBA executive told Beck: "I never thought those two were going to fit together. I just don't know how you run an offense with two power forwards. Neither one of them can shoot and operate in the same space."

Every NBA Team's Biggest Problem Right Now 😠

Ranking Every NBA Team's Top Trade Assets 💪

Antetokounmpo has served as the Heat's leading scorer by averaging 28.4 points through his first seven games in Miami.

That has coincided with Adebayo seeing both his production (20.1 to 16.3 points per game) and usage rate (24.8 percent to 21.4 percent) drop from last season.

Former Heat star and current VP of basketball development Udonis Haslem said he recently had a conversation with Adebayo about how to avoid getting stifled by defenders already working on Antetokounmpo.

"When Giannis busts out... try to get ahead of him, or get across the court from him. Do not trail him. That is the best thing for Bam," Haslam said on Amazon Prime's NBA Nightcap .

Adebayo himself has said he is still working on being more "aggressive" while complementing Antetokounmpo.

The Heat surrendered multiple players who played key roles last season including Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware and Jaime Jaquez Jr. in the trade to acquire Antetokounmpo from the Milwaukee Bucks.

Finding a better fit between Antetokounmpo and Adebayo will be key to the Heat's hopes of adjusting from those roster losses early this season. That will start Wednesday night with the first game of a back-to-back against the LA Clippers and Golden State Warriors.

articles.title: Kon Knueppel expected to make season debut Wednesday
articles.summary: After missing the first eight games to begin the year, Kon Knueppel is expected to make his 2026-27 season debut Wednesday for the Charlotte Hornets.
articles.body:
After one year at Duke, Kon Knueppel had an incredible rookie campaign with the Charlotte Hornets , leading the NBA in 3-pointers made as a rookie while shooting 42.5% from beyond the arc.

Entering the 2026-27 NBA season, hopes were high for Knueppel to continue where he left off. Ahead of training camp, the Hornets revealed that Knueppel suffered a hamstring injury, which kept him out of Charlotte's first eight games of the year.

After a lengthy rehab process, the former No. 4 overall pick appears ready to return. Prior to Charlotte's next matchup Wednesday against the Brooklyn Nets , Knueppel has been listed as probable .

His return couldn't come at a better time for the Hornets, who currently rank dead last in both field goal percentage and points per game. A season ago, the Wisconsin native averaged 18.5 points, 5.3 rebounds, 3.4 assists, and 0.7 steals.

articles.title: Shaquille O’Neal says Michael Jordan’s Chicago Bulls teammate was just ‘along for the ride’ in six Championship wins
articles.summary: Shaquille O’Neal has made a major admission about Scottie Pippen’s stint with the Chicago Bulls. Drafted by the franchise in 1987, Pippen became a key piece...
articles.body:
Shaquille O'Neal has made a major admission about Scottie Pippen's stint with the Chicago Bulls.

Drafted by the franchise in 1987, Pippen became a key piece in the Bulls' dominance in the 90s. He played second fiddle to Michael Jordan but had big responsibilities, which included guarding the best player on the opposing team.

Pippen was alongside Jordan in all six of his championship runs, and many recognise him as one of the greatest second options to ever play in the NBA.

Many rate his achievements immensely high, and while talking about Pippen on The Rushmore podcast, Ari Emanuel had nothing but praise for the Hall of Famer.

He even went as far as saying that Pippen was the greatest small forward to ever play the game, ironically right in front of Kevin Durant, who also plays the same position.

It was then that O'Neal had to jump in and make a strong point about Pippen. The four-time NBA champion said: "Michael got six and Scottie was along the ride."

Durant was also not in agreement with Emanuel's greatest SF comment about Pippen. The 38-year-old picked LeBron James as one of the players who was better than Pippen.

Now Durant and O'Neal both agreed that Pippen was a great player, but it was the greatest SF comment that seemed to bother them.

Although he has six rings to his name, LeBron James has so much more on his resume to clearly run away with the title of the greatest SF of all time.

As far as his importance to the Bulls is concerned, there is no doubt the dynasty would not have been as successful as it was without Pippen. Before his arrival in the league, Jordan had been swept twice in the playoffs and had won only one game, which shows how much he relied on Pippen.

articles.title: Sold-out arenas, 3.3 million viewers for Game 7: The WNBA postseason surges in numbers
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — The WNBA Finals was the most watched since 1999 with an average of 1.88 million people viewing the seven-game series that Golden State won ov...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — The WNBA Finals was the most watched since 1999 with an average of 1.88 million people viewing the seven-game series that Golden State won over Atlanta in a decisive Game 7 .

That game averaged 3.3 million viewers, making it the most watched WNBA postseason game ever. It was up 128% from last season's clinching game between Las Vegas and Phoenix that the Aces won.

All seven games in the series were sold out, including Game 6, which was played at 12:30 p.m. EDT .

The Finals capped the WNBA's most-watched postseason since its inaugural season in 1997, averaging 1.49 million viewers, up 27% from last year.

articles.title: How Cooper Flagg is fast becoming Mavericks' leader at 19
articles.summary: With the teenage star's continued trajectory, Dallas' future is much brighter than its recent past.
articles.body:
DALLAS — Not long after an emotional NBA Cup win over the Houston Rockets on Friday, Cooper Flagg was asked about the joys of the Dallas' Mavericks' new two-star dynamic. Flagg and Kyrie Irving had combined for 68 points, 15 assists and 13 rebounds in the contest, the Mavs' third win in a row. But the 19-year-old didn't want to focus on himself or take away from his team's achievement against a legitimate contender.

Flagg redirected the question to preach about players excelling in their various roles regardless of perceived status.

Such a remark can be lost in a postgame interview, especially one where the subject tends to keep things brief and direct. But in that moment, Flagg was displaying a level of leadership that is typically unbeknownst to teenagers, much less budding superstars being handed the keys to a franchise.

In three months, it will mark two years since the stunning Dallas trade that sent Luka Dončić to Los Angeles in exchange for Anthony Davis. The massive void left by Dončić and the emotional toll from such a jarring move created a butterfly effect for the city and organization, ultimately leading to the drafting of Flagg, but also the firing of head coach Jason Kidd and general manager Nico Harrison, and the hiring of Dusty May and Masai Ujiri this offseason.

But beauty can emerge from despair. So when May and Ujiri embraced in the tunnel after the final buzzer against Houston, hope re-emerged. And although the transition between eras has certainly come with its fair share of detours, Flagg's growing leadership in Year 2 — and, more importantly, his veteran teammates empowering him — has provided a North Star to follow.

"He's taken a step into a leadership role," teammate Daniel Gafford said. "There's different ways you can lead in certain areas. With Coop, he just finds ways to have fun throughout the craziest times. Kyrie [Irving] is one of the biggest leaders in the locker room and he leads by his voice and example. Coop is following suit and taking notes and doing it himself."

"It's huge," Flagg added. "Just getting the respect of my peers and teammates last year was big for me. They're trusting me, I'm trusting myself. It's a good recipe."

Flagg's mental growth has been concurrent with his on-court development. In the shot clock era, there are only 20 players who have averaged 25 points, 5 rebounds, 5 assists, a steal and a block per game. At 19, Flagg is the youngest ever to reach those benchmarks.

Ironically, part of his success stems from the chaos he was born into. As a rookie under Kidd, Flagg was originally miscast as a point guard with questionable spacing at times, and at other junctures shared a backcourt with the likes of Brandon Williams, Ryan Nembhard and D'Angelo Russell — hardly a trio of names that screams development. Flagg also was a victim of Dallas' rotational roulette; only Cleveland and Washington had their most common lineups on the floor together less than Flagg's most consistent one (92 minutes, per NBA.com tracking data) last season.

A year later, Flagg has a clear-cut role in a cleaner half-court setup and has taken lessons from his playmaking past and refined them. His processor has sped up as the game has slowed down for him, better understanding how to attack opposing defenders, crack open schemes and create the best shot for himself and those around him.

As his usage rate has risen, so too has his assist rate, with Flagg now operating in the 98th and 97th percentiles , respectively, per Cleaning the Glass. An increase in possessions as a ball-handler has resulted in top-20 marks in secondary assists, potential assists and assist points created. It's no surprise the Mavericks are 17 points per 100 half-court possessions better with Flagg on the floor.

Flip to a Mavs game on League Pass on a Tuesday night and you'll see Irving receive an inbounds pass, flip it to Flagg and jog to the opposing wing to let him go to work.

"Just comfortable," Flagg said on how he feels with the ball in the half-court. "I'm comfortable getting to my spots and with my teammates. Coach is putting me in great spots."

Dallas was one of the worst spacing units last season, but Flagg now has Irving (a career 40% 3-point shooter) and Max Christie (38%) next to him (and the hope is P.J. Washington returns to his 2024 form, where he shot 38% from deep). May also wants to play with pace and incorporates a high volume of pick-and-rolls to get both Flagg and Irving on the ball. The pace, space and freedom allow Flagg's unorthodox style to take form — more isolations , more midrange attempts and a better overall shot selection. (His 3-point efficiency, hovering around 23%, remains a work in progress, but he's been able to establish elite go-to moves that negate the need to launch unnecessary 3s into the sun.)

Flagg's improved comfort within the offense speaks to his relationship with May; an open, honest one that incorporates feedback and fluidity.

"It's been great," Flagg said of his bond with May. "He watched a ton of film from last year and knows my game pretty well. So just whatever he's seeing where he wants to put me, it's been working really well."

Still, arguably none of this is made possible without Irving's presence, patience and poise. For starters, his gravity alone makes Flagg's job easier on a nightly basis, drawing attention away from him and opening up more space to operate. But Irving's experience, having shared the spotlight with a plethora of big names during his tenure, makes the day-to-day easier as well. For what it's worth, the Mavericks have outscored opponents by 25 points in 98 minutes that Flagg and Irving have been on the floor together. It's been less of a turn-by-turn approach and more cooperative, with Irving wanting to push Flagg to be the best version of himself. As an elder statesman now, it's about giving back to the younger generation.

"It's been great," Irving said to Yahoo Sports. "In my first few years in the league, I had some good veterans — Anthony Parker, Antawn Jamison, Anderson Varejão — they were all good to me. But I was always trying to figure out what more I can do to bring to the team, and the best thing for me was being able to be honest about who I wanted to become in this league and how I was gonna accomplish it. It wasn't a solo job. I think he has a lot more patience than I did when I was his age. With the supporting cast around him, he can trust us with any information or questions he wants to ask."

It takes a village to raise young players. A head coach without NBA experience forced to lean on his roster, creativity and communication. A wily, sage veteran with championship experience that is hell-bent on pouring into the next phase of NBA basketball. A community that supports and sees the full potential of an ascending superstar.

There's still work to do. The Mavericks, despite their winning record, are just 18th in net rating. And it's not just their conference that remains a gauntlet; their own division — with the Rockets, Spurs and Grizzlies ahead of them — is as deep as ever. But with Flagg's continued trajectory , along with the other now-stable pieces in place, Dallas' future is much brighter than its recent past.

"There's always so much room for improvement," Flagg said. "I haven't shot the ball incredibly well behind the arc. But just continuing to play at my own pace, getting better and cleaning up the turnovers. There's always room for improvement."

articles.title: Warriors reportedly not paying Kristaps Porziņģis as he contemplates NBA future
articles.summary: The Warriors aren't looking into voiding the contract as they are hoping to move him before the Feb. 11 trade deadline.
articles.body:
Kristaps Porziņģis is reportedly not being paid any of his $20 million salary by the Golden State Warriors since he is not playing, according to ESPN's Shams Charania and Anthony Slater .

Porziņģis, who is away from the team as he deals with recurring POTS (Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome) symptoms, remains in play as the Warriors seek to move the 31-year-old forward before the Feb. 11 NBA trade deadline as they continue not paying him.

There are reportedly no plans for the Warriors to void Porziņģis' contract and the player is not disputing the lack of payments. He signed a two-year, $40 million contract in the summer with only $3 million guaranteed in the second season of the deal.

According to Bobby Marks , the decision is costing Porziņģis $218,341 per game.

Porziņģis released a statement last month saying that he was working with doctors to find a way back to better health after Charania reported the veteran was contemplating his future.

According to Cleveland Clinic , "POTS is a condition that causes your heart to beat faster than normal when you go from sitting or lying down to standing up." Symptoms can vary widely from patient to patient, but Porziņģis' seem more respiratory and fatigue-related.

POTS significantly limited the 7-foot-2 Porziņģis during the 2024-25 Eastern Conference semifinals against the New York Knicks, when he was with the Boston Celtics.

Porziņģis averaged just 15.5 minutes in that six-game series, which ended Boston's NBA title defense, with Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla revealing after Game 5 that Porziņģis didn't play the second half because " he couldn't breathe ."

Over his 10-year career, Porziņģis has played 533 games and has averaged 19.5 points, 7.6 rebounds, and 1.9 assists per game.

Last season, he split time between the Atlanta Hawks and the Warriors, appearing in 32 games, the fewest he's played in a season in his career, outside of the missed 2018-19 campaign.

articles.title: Olivier Rioux becomes tallest player to start a Division 1 basketball game, dunks from behind basket
articles.summary: Olivier Rioux is poised to see far more playing time with UC Irvine.
articles.body:
For much of his college-basketball career, Olivier Rioux has been more of an idea than a reality. He received plenty of attention for his height, but that didn't translate the much playing time at Florida.

Because of that, Rioux transferred to UC Irvine in April, where he was expected to see the court more. The 7-foot-9 center got his wish Tuesday, earning his first-ever college start. In doing so, he broke a record, becoming the tallest player to start a Division 1 basketball game

It proved to be worth the wait, as Rioux posted a double-double in the contest, scoring 13 points and pulling down 12 rebounds in a 92-66 win over Chapman.

Rioux's performance also included a mind-bending highlight, in which the center dunked the ball despite the majority of his body being behind the basket.

It didn't even look that difficult for Rioux, who casually hopped up and dunked the ball. That's the benefit of being 7-foot-9, apparently.

With UC Irvine, Rioux finally has an opportunity to show his height can translate on the court. After redshirting at Florida as a freshman, Rioux was used sparingly by the program last season, averaging just 1.5 minutes per game across 11 contests. Throughout his entire career at Florida, Rioux was just three of six from the field, with six rebounds and seven points. He exceeded those figures in his game at UC Irvine.

Rioux still has a long way to go before his production puts him on NBA Draft radars. His 7-foot-9 frame should get him attention, but height can only get a player so far in the pros. Despite being 7-foot-6, Tacko Fall has yet to establish himself as a consistent NBA player.

Still, Rioux's size is notable. At 7-foot-9, he would be the tallest player to play in an NBA game if his career reached that point.

That's far from a guarantee, but at least Rioux now has the opportunity show what he can do.
